title: Majority Element
interviewTips: Ask if a majority element is guaranteed to exist: problem 169 guarantees it, so Boyer-Moore needs no verification pass, otherwise add a second counting pass.
Trade-off discussion: HashMap is most intuitive O(n) time O(n) space, Sorting is concise O(n log n) time O(1) extra, Boyer-Moore is optimal O(n) time O(1) space but less obvious.
Edge cases to mention: n=1 single element, all elements same, negative numbers and zeros, majority at start vs end; test with [1] and [2,2,1,1,1,2,2].

approaches.name: Approach 1: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: For each distinct value, count how many times it appears by scanning the whole array. The first value with count greater than n/2 is the answer. Direct translation of the definition of majority.
approaches.theory: Majority means frequency > floor(n/2). Outer loop picks a candidate x, inner loop computes its exact frequency. Since a majority is guaranteed, some x will pass the threshold. This is correct but repeats work for duplicates, leading to quadratic time.

timeComplexity.explanation: For each of n elements we scan all n elements to count, so n * n operations.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Only counters and loop variables, no extra data structure.

edgeCases: All same [2,2,2] returns on first candidate
TLE on large n due to quadratic time

approaches.name: Approach 2: Hash Map Counting
approaches.intuition: Count frequencies in one pass with a dictionary. As soon as any count exceeds n/2 we can return early because only the majority can reach that threshold.
approaches.theory: Use hash table num -> frequency. Incrementally maintain counts. By pigeonhole principle at most one key can exceed n/2. Early exit keeps average work low. Correct whether or not majority is guaranteed, with final fallback if needed.

timeComplexity.explanation: Single pass over n elements, average O(1) hash insert and lookup per element.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Hash map stores up to n distinct keys in worst case.

edgeCases: Negative numbers and large ints work as hash keys
Early exit saves time when majority appears early

approaches.name: Approach 3: Sorting
approaches.intuition: If we sort the array, all equal values become contiguous. Since the majority occupies more than half the slots, it must occupy the middle index n/2.
approaches.theory: Let m be majority with freq > n/2. After sorting, the segment of m has length > n/2, so any window of size > n/2 must intersect it, in particular index floor(n/2) must be m. This holds for both odd and even n. Sorting dominates cost.

timeComplexity.explanation: Dominated by comparison sort of n elements.

spaceComplexity.explanation: In-place sort uses O(1) extra besides O(log n) recursion stack in C++ and Java; Python Timsort uses O(n) worst-case but in-place sort idea is O(1) extra.

edgeCases: Mutates input order, copy first if original order must be preserved

approaches.name: Approach 4: Optimal Boyer-Moore Majority Vote
approaches.intuition: Pair up different elements and cancel them. Since majority has more copies than all others combined, it cannot be fully cancelled and survives as the candidate.
approaches.theory: Maintain candidate and count. If count is 0, take current as candidate. If current equals candidate increment count else decrement count. This simulates cancellation: each decrement pairs a candidate vote with a different vote. Non-majority votes cancel at most 1-for-1, so true majority with > n/2 votes must remain. Needs no extra memory and one pass when existence is guaranteed, otherwise add verification pass.

timeComplexity.explanation: Single linear scan, O(1) work per element.

edgeCases: If majority not guaranteed, add second pass to verify candidate frequency > n/2 else return -1
